edition: Discover — 27 November 2026 · Secret Rooms and Drowned Songs
intro: Hidden chambers, a disputed UFO crash and the songs of Patchface lead this edition. There is a complete dark-fantasy reprint to read, two substantial horror RPG reviews, and fresh reflections on saints, worship and hospitality. Archive picks and retrospectives are labelled; major spoilers are flagged.

items.title: 52 years on, the Carbondale UFO incident continues to intrigue
items.summary: A fresh retrospective on a glowing Pennsylvania pond and a supposed 1974 UFO crash. It recounts the witnesses, crowds and recovered railroad lantern, then explains why a cover-up interpretation persists despite evidence of a hoax.
items.why: A compact Why Files-style puzzle: a striking sight, a mundane object and a legend that survives its apparent explanation.

items.title: The Ghost Room: Family secrets and haunted houses
items.summary: Alvin Nicholas explores secret chambers, priest holes and haunted rooms in British houses. Genuine architectural hiding places sit alongside legends of imprisoned relatives and apparitions; he also asks whether ghost stories sometimes discouraged people from discovering family secrets.
items.why: Hidden rooms give this collection a satisfying physical mystery beneath the folklore. The possibility that a haunting protected a real secret is especially intriguing.

items.title: St. Francis and the Grammar of Gratitude
items.summary: Chad Engelland reads Francis through Chesterton, exploring gratitude as a response to creation understood as gift. The essay argues that Christian belief can deepen appreciation of ordinary goods and existence itself.
items.why: A philosophical way into a familiar saint, connecting praise, love and the goodness of being. Chesterton’s account of receiving the world is a rewarding thread to pursue.

items.title: Fear & Hunger
items.summary: An October retrospective review of the older dungeon crawler, examining how scarcity, dangerous saving and costly combat create dread through systems. Aleks Franiczek praises its cohesive design while questioning its excesses. Contains gameplay and lore spoilers, graphic violence and sexual content.
items.why: For your interest in horror RPGs, this asks how a turn-based game can make each decision frightening. It is substantial criticism of both its ingenuity and its abrasive extremes.

items.title: The Grinning Woman
items.summary: A complete supernatural story by Michael Kelly: a return to a family cottage revives a childhood terror and tales of creatures from the deep. This is a reprint of a story originally published in Nightmare Abbey, Issue 10, March 2026; the date records that original publication.
items.why: An older gem to read in one sitting, with lakeside storytelling, thin places and the uneasy possibility that a family’s tall tales conceal something real.

items.title: The Heart of Culture Is Worship: Recovering Our Catholic and Classical Tradition
items.summary: Daniel Fitzpatrick considers classical learning and Christian culture, beginning with Tertullian’s question about Athens and Jerusalem. He contrasts Greek ideals of education and argues for formation directed toward sanctity, language and reason.
items.why: A longer theological argument linking literature, philosophy and the kind of people a culture forms. It offers plenty to examine alongside your interest in Christianity’s intellectual tradition.

items.title: House of Necrosis
items.summary: An October review of a 2025 game mixing Resident Evil’s mansion horror with Mystery Dungeon’s turn-based exploration. Ben Love examines ammunition scarcity, cramped inventories and shifting corridors behind its PlayStation-style presentation. Contains mechanics and enemy spoilers.
items.why: A particularly appealing crossover of your retro and horror interests: familiar 32-bit atmosphere with tactical decisions driving the tension. The review explains why the combination works beyond nostalgia.

items.title: Haunted Ross-on-Wye: Ghosts and Paranormal Tales from Herefordshire
items.summary: A recent survey of local legends around Goodrich Castle, Penyard woods, old inns and the River Wye. Spectral huntsmen, monks and travellers are presented as the area’s reported folklore rather than demonstrated events.
items.why: A fireside collection with a strong sense of place: wooded landscapes, ruined castles and coaching inns make a change from laboratory-style paranormal investigations.

items.title: A Labor of Love: The Communion of a Home‑Cooked Meal
items.summary: Madison Ayers reflects on preparing meals for friends and family as an act of hospitality and love. She connects the work of feeding others with communion, the Last Supper and the human meaning of eating together.
items.why: A quieter counterpoint to the mysteries, bringing theology into an ordinary creative act. It explores how care becomes tangible through time, craft and a shared table.

items.category: A Song of Ice and Fire · older gem
items.title: The Prophecies of Patchface
items.summary: Archive pick from 6 October 2025. History of Westeros interprets the drowned fool’s disturbing songs, his associations with shadows and the sea, and Melisandre’s fear of him. These are fan readings of the books’ mysteries, not confirmed answers. Major spoilers through the published ASOIAF novels.
items.why: Where your spooky and Westeros interests meet: a seemingly marginal character whose rhymes invite close reading and unsettling theories. Ideal for a slower lore session.
